715.title: Mara comes
715.hook: Mara with his bow of flowers and his army of horrors (Buddhacarita 13)
715.howItsDone: Mara's attack on the seated Buddha is painted and carved in Buddhist art, and some Buddhist teachers speak of Mara as a name for whatever in the mind pulls a person away from awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nandabala's milk, and the prince's strength returning. Your line: strength returns.

Flowers on the bow. Flowers on the arrows. The figure who comes for the prince doesn't look like a monster at first. He looks like desire itself, and that's who he is. The prince has eaten, bathed, and walked to a great tree, and he has sat down beneath it, resolved not to get up until he has found what he's looking for. The poem says the whole world grew glad at that. Except one. In his own realm, Mara trembles.
screen: `FLOWERS ON THE BOW.` → `HE SITS, RESOLVED.` → `ONLY MARA TREMBLES.`

segments.voice: First, who Mara is. The poem gives him two names at once. In the world he is called the god of love, the one with the flowered bow. And he is also Mara, the enemy of freedom. Ashvaghosha joins them on purpose: the one who makes us want and the one who keeps us bound are, in this poem, the same figure. Second, his fear. His sons and daughters ask why he's troubled. That man under the tree, he says, has put on the armor of resolve. If he wins, he'll lead others out of my realm, and it will stand empty. So I'll break his vow before he finishes. Third, the bow. Mara goes to the tree with his children and speaks first. Get up, he says, in paraphrase. You're a warrior by birth. Go back to your duty, rule, make offerings, win heaven the proper way. Give up this begging road. If you won't rise, here's my arrow. He lets it fly. The prince doesn't stir. He doesn't even seem to notice it. Fourth, the army. Mara is shaken, and changes weapons: if desire won't work, fear might. He calls up his army, and the poem fills the air around the tree with horrors, creatures with the faces of beasts, many-armed, many-headed, carrying spears, clubs, swords and burning trees, howling, surrounding the seated man on every side. That's where the poem leaves him today. Notice the order of attack. The soft weapon first: the appeal to duty, to sense, to pleasure. Only when the flower arrow fails does Mara reach for the horrors.
screen: `THE GOD OF LOVE, THE ENEMY OF FREEDOM.` · `IF HE WINS, MY REALM IS EMPTY.` · `THE FLOWER ARROW DOES NOTHING.` · `AN ARMY OF HORRORS.` · then, large: `THE BOW OF FLOWERS.`

segments.voice: Let the body be as still as you comfortably can, like someone seated beneath a tree, and let one fear come forward, not the biggest, just one that's around today. Name it quietly in a few words, the way you'd name a bird you can see: this is the fear of not having enough. Then let the breath stay slow, and keep sitting; you don't have to fight it.
Mara comes. The god of desire and enemy of freedom shoots his flower arrow at the seated prince, and when it fails, calls up an army of horrors. Today's word.
Your line: the bow of flowers. The soft pull comes before the army. Day seven hundred fifteen.

recall: the prince, unmoved in the garden

chat.says: Why does Mara shoot a flower arrow before sending his army?
options: He's desire too: he tries the soft pull first, and fear only after.
Flowers were his only weapons until the gods gave him an army.
He wanted to honor the prince with flowers before the battle.
chat.meaning: The poem makes the god of love and Mara one figure. The soft weapon comes first; the army of horrors only when the arrow fails.

Mara.meaning: the tempter, enemy of freedom, who tries to stop the awakening

god of love.meaning: the name the world gives Mara, with his flowered bow

Ashvaghosha.meaning: the poet tradition names for the Buddhacarita

716.title: Mara defeated
716.hook: the army scatters; a voice from the sky tells Mara to give up (Buddhacarita 13)
716.howItsDone: Buddhist art shows the Buddha seated at the moment of victory over Mara, and in some traditions the story is retold at festivals of the awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mara comes, first with a flower arrow, then with an army. Your line: the bow of flowers.

The army doesn't stop to talk. Mara has already tried talking: a speech about duty, a flower arrow, and the man under the tree didn't stir. So now everything the army can lift, it throws. Rocks, trees, spears, fire. The air around the tree fills with howling and smoke. In the middle of it, one man sits with his legs crossed and his eyes steady. He doesn't answer. He doesn't flinch. And then a voice speaks from somewhere above the noise, from someone nobody can see.
screen: `ROCKS, TREES, SPEARS, FIRE.` → `ONE MAN, SITTING STILL.` → `A VOICE FROM ABOVE.`

segments.voice: First, the attack. The poem gives the army full force. Some hurl boulders. Some swing whole trees. Some throw weapons, some breathe fire, some try to terrify him with shrieks and faces. Second, what happens to it. Nothing lands. In paraphrase, what's thrown at him stops in the air, or falls short, or turns harmless. The fire doesn't burn him. The noise doesn't move him. Third, the voice. A being in the sky, unseen, speaks to Mara: give up this useless effort. Lay down your anger. You can no more shake this man than the wind can shake the great mountain. Fire might lose its heat, water its wetness, the earth its firmness, before he gives up his resolve. He has made his vow, and the time has come for it to be fulfilled. Fourth, the scattering. Mara looks at the man under the tree, still unmoved, and the poem says he goes away disheartened, his effort spent, and his army scatters in every direction. The sky clears. Flowers fall from it. Look at how the victory is won. The prince never lifts a hand, never argues back, never calls for help. The poem doesn't even give him a line. His whole answer is to keep sitting, and the army, which could break anything that resisted, has nothing to push against. What scatters it isn't a stronger army. It's stillness that won't be moved.
screen: `THE ARMY THROWS EVERYTHING.` · `NOTHING LANDS.` · `NO WIND SHAKES THE MOUNTAIN.` · `MARA GOES, DISHEARTENED.` · then, large: `THE ARMY SCATTERS.`

segments.voice: Bring back the fear you named yesterday, or another that's here today, and let it come close without pushing it away or following it. Keep sitting, the way the prince keeps sitting while the army howls, and feel the breath come in and go out underneath it. If the fear thins, let it thin; if it stays, that's all right, and keep breathing.
Mara defeated. The army throws everything at the seated prince and nothing lands; a voice from the sky tells Mara to give up, and his army scatters. Today's word.
Your line: the army scatters. Tomorrow the night goes on, and the poem turns from what he refused to what he sees. That's day seven hundred sixteen.

what a scholar hears: Ashvaghosha gives the victory no speech from the prince at all, so his steadiness is the whole answer, likened to a mountain no wind can move.

chat.says: How did the prince beat Mara's army if he never fought back?
options: He kept sitting; nothing landed, and the army had nothing to push against.
A god in the sky fought for him and struck the whole army down.
He bargained with Mara, promising to go back to the palace later.
chat.meaning: In the poem he never lifts a hand or speaks. What's thrown stops or turns harmless, and his stillness can't be moved.

Mara.meaning: the tempter, enemy of freedom, who tries to stop the awakening

great mountain.meaning: the voice's image for the prince: the wind can't shake it

717.title: Perfect knowledge
717.hook: the night of awakening, told in verse (Buddhacarita 14)
717.howItsDone: The awakening is remembered at Vesak (or Wesak), when in many places temples are lit and people gather to meditate, keep precepts and hear teachings; in some places devotees sit through the night in memory of the night under the tree.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mara defeated. The army threw everything, nothing landed, and your line was the army scatters. Now the field is empty, and the night is still young.

The noise is over. Mara's army, the arrows, the shrieking shapes, is gone. What's left is a man under a tree, and a night ahead of him. A story could stop here, with the victory. The poem doesn't. It slows down and walks through the dark one stretch at a time, the way someone who can't sleep feels every hour of a long night. The battle was loud. The awakening, in Ashvaghosha's telling, is quiet, and it takes all night.
screen: `THE BATTLE IS OVER.` → `A MAN UNDER A TREE.` → `THE NIGHT, HOUR BY HOUR.`

segments.voice: First, he looks back. In the first watch of the night, the poem says, he remembers his own former lives, one after another: where he was born, what his name was, what happened to him. What he feels, looking back, is not pride. It's compassion, for every being caught in that long turning. Second, he looks out. In the middle watch, the poem gives him a clear, divine sight. He sees beings everywhere dying and being born again, rising and falling according to what they have done. The whole world seems to him to have no solid core, like the stem of a plantain plant: layers, with nothing hard in the middle. Third, he looks in. In the last watch, he asks the question under all the others: where do old age and death come from? From birth. And birth? From becoming. Link by link, he follows the chain back to not knowing, ignorance. Then he sees it the other way: when ignorance ends, the chain comes apart, link by link, all the way to the end of old age and death. Fourth, the dawn. As the night ends, the poem says, he reaches perfect knowledge. He has become the Buddha, the awakened one. The earth sways, flowers fall, and the gods rejoice. At the center of all that color sits one still figure who has finished a long question. The discourses tell this night more plainly, with the same three watches. The poem adds the beauty. Both share the shape: looking back, looking out, looking in, and then light.
screen: `FIRST WATCH: HIS OWN PAST LIVES.` · `MIDDLE WATCH: ALL BEINGS, COMING AND GOING.` · `LAST WATCH: THE CHAIN OF CAUSES.` · `DAWN: THE AWAKENED ONE.` · then, large: `THE NIGHT OF KNOWING.`

segments.voice: For a few breaths, look back over today, what happened, without judging it. Then look out at the people around you, near and far, each going through their own day, and then look in, at just this breath, coming and going.
Perfect knowledge. Through the watches of one night he remembers, sees and understands, and at dawn he is the Buddha. Today's word.
Your line: the night of knowing. Back, out, in, and then the dawn. Day seven hundred seventeen, done.

chat.says: Did the Buddha wake up the moment Mara ran off?
options: No. In the poem it takes all night: past lives, all beings, then causes.
Yes. The moment Mara left, he woke up, and the night was over.
No. He fasted for years more after Mara before he finally woke up.
chat.meaning: The poem walks through the watches of one night: he remembers, sees and understands, and at dawn reaches perfect knowledge.

Ashvaghosha.meaning: the poet tradition names as author of this life in verse

Mara.meaning: the tempter who tried to stop him under the tree

plantain.meaning: a banana-like plant whose stem is layers with no hard core

Buddha.meaning: one who has woken up, the awakened one

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 14 (the watches of the night, dependent origination, the awakening at dawn)
Majjhima Nikaya 36 (the three knowledges in the three watches)

718.title: The wheel turned
718.hook: the first sermon and the five companions (Buddhacarita 15)
718.howItsDone: The first teaching is remembered in Buddhist communities; in Theravada lands the full moon of Asalha (Asalha Puja) marks it, and the wheel, the dharma-chakra, appears on temple roofs, gates and flags as a sign of the teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: perfect knowledge, a whole night of looking back, out and in, and your line, the night of knowing. Today the Buddha gets up and walks toward people.

Five men in a park near Benares see someone walking toward them, and they make a plan. They know him. They practiced hard beside him once, fasting and straining, until he gave it up and started eating again. They decided he'd gone soft. So as he comes closer, they agree: we won't stand up for him. We won't greet him. Let him sit where he likes. Then he arrives, and the plan doesn't survive the moment.
screen: `FIVE OLD COMPANIONS.` → `A PLAN NOT TO STAND.` → `THEN HE ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: First, the welcome they didn't intend. In the poem, as he draws near, the five find themselves rising anyway. The Vinaya's telling adds the details: one takes his bowl and robe, one brings water, one makes ready a seat. Their agreement falls apart in their hands. They still speak to him as an old friend, by name, and he tells them gently not to: he has become something new. Second, the middle way. What he teaches first is not a list of rules. It's a road between two ditches. On one side, the life of pleasure he left in the palace. On the other, the self-punishment these five still believe in, the starving and the straining. Neither leads to peace, he says. There is a middle path, and it is the one he found. Third, the truths. He names suffering, its arising, its ending, and the path that leads to its ending. And he lays out that path: right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. The poem sets all of this into verse, so the first teaching becomes something you could almost sing. Fourth, the first one who sees. Kaundinya, one of the five, understands. The discourses say that when he did, a cry went up through the heavens: the wheel of the teaching has been set rolling, and no one in the world can turn it back. A wheel, once pushed, keeps rolling. The Buddha gave it the first push, in a deer park, to five men who had planned not to stand up.
screen: `THE FIVE RISE ANYWAY.` · `A ROAD BETWEEN TWO DITCHES.` · `THE TRUTHS AND THE PATH.` · `KAUNDINYA SEES IT.` · then, large: `THE WHEEL, IN VERSE.`

segments.voice: Think of one place where you swing between two ditches, all in or all out, work all night or not at all, and try to say the middle of it in one plain line, the way you'd tell a friend. Not a rule, just a road between the two; then let the line go and rest with the breath.
Dharmacakra, the wheel of the teaching, turned for the first time: the middle way, the truths and the path, taught to five old companions in a deer park, and Kaundinya understands. Today's word.
Your line: the wheel, in verse. Once it was pushed, no one could turn it back. See you tomorrow.

original.note: Sanskrit dharmacakra, the wheel of the teaching (Pali dhammacakka).

what a scholar hears: the Pali discourse that tells it is called the turning of the wheel of the dhamma (SN 56.11); the poem retells it in verse.

That fasting hard enough is the surest way to free the mind of craving.

chat.meaning: To the five, he named two ditches, pleasure and self-torment, then the middle way, the truths and the eightfold path.

Benares.meaning: an old name for Varanasi, a city on the Ganges

Kaundinya.meaning: the first of the five companions to understand

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 15 (the journey to Benares, the five, the first teaching)
Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.6 (the five rise despite their agreement: bowl, water, seat)

719.title: Many come
719.hook: the fire-worshipers, the kings, the friends (Buddhacarita 16)
719.howItsDone: The Fire Sermon is still chanted and taught in Theravada communities, and in some communities monasteries and temples receive newcomers, from curious visitors to people asking to ordain, with a simple welcome and a place to sit.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dharmacakra, the wheel of the teaching, first pushed in a deer park. Your line, the wheel, in verse. Today the wheel starts picking up people.

A rich young man wakes in the middle of the night in a beautiful house. The lamps are still burning. The musicians who played for him have fallen asleep where they sat, sprawled and snoring. Suddenly he sees it all as ugly and sad. If that sounds familiar, it should: it's the prince's night, a few cantos back, happening to someone else. His name is Yasas. He walks out of the house in distress, and he finds the Buddha. And after him, the poem says, his friends come too.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN WAKES AT NIGHT.` → `THE PRINCE'S NIGHT, AGAIN.` → `HE WALKS OUT, AND FRIENDS FOLLOW.`

segments.voice: Canto sixteen is a canto of arrivals. First, the friends. Yasas is taught, and goes forth. His friends hear what he's done and come to see for themselves. The teaching travels the way news often travels: one friend tells another. Second, the fire-worshipers. At Uruvilva lives a famous ascetic of the Kashyapa family, a keeper of sacred fires, with his brothers and a crowd of followers. The Buddha asks to spend the night in the hall where the fire is kept. There's a fierce serpent in there, they warn him. He goes in anyway, and in the morning the serpent lies calm in his bowl. Even so, the story has the eldest brother hold on to his pride for a while, until at last he yields. He and his followers give up their fire rites, and the tradition says they threw their fire gear into the river. Downstream, his brothers see it floating past, and come upriver to find out what happened. Third, the fire sermon. To these fire-keepers the Buddha speaks in their own language: everything is burning. The eye is burning, the ear, the mind, with the fires of desire, anger and delusion. People who tended fire all their lives hear about a fire they can put out. Fourth, the king. In Rajagriha, King Bimbisara, who once offered the young wanderer half a kingdom, hears he has come back. The prince had promised to return once he found what he was looking for, and he keeps the promise. The king comes out to listen, and is moved. Friends, fire-keepers, a king. Many come.
screen: `YASAS, THEN HIS FRIENDS.` · `THE KEEPERS OF THE FIRE.` · `EVERYTHING IS BURNING.` · `A KING, AND A PROMISE KEPT.` · then, large: `MANY COME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone new somewhere you already belong, a coworker, a neighbor, a new face in a class or a place of worship, and picture the door they walked through as it looks from their side. Hold them there with a plain, friendly wish, and rest with the breath.
Many come. Yasas and his friends, the Kashyapa brothers with their fire, and King Bimbisara, all arriving in one canto. Today's word.
Your line: everything is burning. And a fire that burns can also be put out. Day seven hundred nineteen.

720.title: Mahakassapa comes
720.hook: the great ascetic comes to him (Buddhacarita 17)
720.howItsDone: Mahakassapa is honored in Theravada as a model of forest and ascetic practice, and in Zen lineages as the first heir of the teaching after the Buddha. Monks in forest traditions still keep some of the strict practices he is remembered for.

segments.voice: Yesterday: many come, friends, fire-keepers and a king, and your line, everything is burning. Today one more arrives, a man who had already given up nearly everything.

Two robes on a roadside. One is a patched outer robe, but soft, folded into a seat under a tree. The other is rough hemp, worn thin, stitched together from rags. In a little while, the two men wearing them will swap. The man with the soft robe is a seeker who has already left a wealthy home. The man with the rags is the Buddha. This is how the discourses remember the meeting with Kassapa, later called Mahakassapa, great Kassapa. And the poem, in its seventeenth canto, sends him walking toward the Buddha too.
screen: `TWO ROBES ON A ROADSIDE.` → `ONE SOFT, ONE RAGGED.` → `KASSAPA IS COMING.`

segments.voice: First, what he left. Tradition remembers Kassapa as born into a wealthy brahmin family, and leaving it all, house, riches, a wife, to go looking for freedom. Later tradition adds a tender detail: his wife, Bhadda, wanted the same thing, and the two of them went forth together, parting at a crossroads to walk different roads. Second, the meeting. In his own words in the discourses, Kassapa says he saw the Buddha sitting by a shrine on the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda, and knew at once: this is my teacher. He bowed and said so, and the Buddha taught him there by the road. Third, the robes. Kassapa folded his cloak for the Buddha to sit on. The Buddha remarked how soft it was. Kassapa offered it, and the Buddha gave him his own worn rag-robe in return. It's a small, strange exchange, and some readers take it as a sign: the teacher handing his robe to someone who would carry the teaching on. Fourth, what he became. The discourses list Kassapa as foremost among the monks who kept the strict ascetic practices: living in the forest, eating only alms food, wearing rag-robes. He came after the first five, after Yasas and the fire-keepers. He wasn't the first. But in the stories, he became one of the great ones, and tradition says that after the Buddha's death it was Kassapa who called the monks together to remember what had been taught. The great ones don't all arrive at the start.
screen: `A WEALTHY HOME, LEFT BEHIND.` · `THIS IS MY TEACHER.` · `A SOFT CLOAK FOR A RAG-ROBE.` · `FOREMOST IN THE STRICT PRACTICES.` · then, large: `THE GREAT ONES ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who joined something after you did, a family, a team, a circle of friends, and who may never have felt part of the founding story. Notice one thing they carry now that no one else does, and rest with the breath, holding them in that light.

721.title: The rest of the poem
721.hook: the full poem survives in Tibetan and Chinese, carrying the story to the relics
721.howItsDone: English translations of the full Buddhacarita follow the Sanskrit where it survives and the Tibetan or Chinese versions after that; the Buddha's relics are honored at stupas across Asia.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mahakassapa comes, a soft cloak traded for a rag-robe. Your line, the great ones arrive. Today, the end of the poem's road.

A book with its last chapters torn out, and a friend overseas who happens to own a copy. That's roughly the situation with this poem. The Sanskrit text, the language Ashvaghosha wrote in, breaks off partway through the story. If that were all there was, the life in verse would stop in the middle of the night under the tree, before the dawn. But the poem was carried abroad and translated, into Tibetan and into Chinese, and in those versions the story keeps going, all the way to the end.
screen: `A BOOK WITH ITS LAST PAGES GONE.` → `THE SANSKRIT BREAKS OFF.` → `TIBETAN AND CHINESE CARRY ON.`

segments.voice: So what's in the rest of the poem? Four stretches. First, a gift of land. A rich merchant, Anathapindika, buys a prince's grove for the Buddha and the monks, so they have a place to stay through the rains. The teaching has a home. Second, the return. The Buddha goes back to his father's city, the one he left through the silent gates. The king who tried to keep him in meets a son who comes back as a teacher, and listens. Third, the trouble and the welcome. A cousin, Devadatta, turns against him and sets a maddened elephant loose in his path, and the elephant stops and grows calm before him. And a courtesan, Amrapali, welcomes him into her mango grove and gives it to the community. The poem honors her gift. Fourth, the end. The Buddha, old and ill, makes his last journey, lies down between two sala trees at Kushinagara, gives his last teaching, and passes into final nirvana. Near its close the poem goes one step further than the death: the kings of the region quarrel over his relics, nearly go to war, and then agree to share them, each carrying a portion home to honor. So the story closes with the life scattered across many places, and kept. Notice the echo. The poem had the same fate: scattered, carried, kept in other languages. This week ran from Mara's bow of flowers, through his defeat, the night of knowing, dharmacakra, many coming and Mahakassapa, to the rest of the poem, carried home by other hands.
